title: The Mathematics and Physics Splitting Graph
takeaway: Three autoencoders of increasing width, trained on the same one-layer transformer, are lined up side by side, and the technical-writing features of the smallest run are traced into their relatives in the larger ones. The descriptions attached to those relatives get narrower as the dictionary grows: one feature for mathematical prose becomes separate features for category theory, complex analysis, field theory and machine learning. The links are set by a quantitative similarity measure, but "more specific" is read off the feature descriptions rather than scored.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Three columns, one per [[dictionary-learning-run]] — a separately trained [[sparse-autoencoder]] on the same transformer's MLP activations, differing only in how many features it is allowed to learn. Left to right: $512$, $4{,}096$, $16{,}384$. Each dark box is one learned feature. Its label is the paper's [[feature-notation]] (model / run / index), and the line under it is a short human description of what that feature fires on.

### How to read it

The lines between columns are not drawn by hand. For each pair of features the paper computes a [[masked-cosine-similarity]]: take the [[feature-activation]] of both across tokens, restrict to the tokens where the first one fires, and take the cosine similarity there. Repeat restricted to where the second fires. Keep the larger of the two numbers.

A line is drawn when that number exceeds about $0.4$. The threshold is admittedly a display choice — small enough graph to look at, rich enough to show structure. Features in the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] are dropped first.

Pink lines descend from `A/0/281`, purple from `A/0/341`. Colour is only ancestry.

### What it shows

Read any left-hand box against the boxes it points to. `A/0/341` is "the" in mathematical prose — one of the paper's [[token-in-context-features]]. In `A/1` its territory is covered by three features: "the" in machine learning, "the" in topology and complex analysis, and "a" in math. In `A/2` those divide again, into complex analysis versus topology and abstract algebra.

That is [[feature-splitting]] run as a sweep rather than shown once: same model, same procedure, only the dictionary size varied.

One box breaks the tree. `A/1/512` receives both a pink and a purple line, so it descends from both `A/0` features at once — features merge as well as split, which is the paper's point that [[splitting-is-not-a-tree]].

The paper offers one corroboration beyond the descriptions. The [[logit-weight]] tops for the coarse `A/0/341` are generic — *the denominator*, *the theorem*. For `A/2/15021` they are topical — *the dataset*, *the classifier*; for `A/2/4878`, *the quotient*, *the subgroup*.

Note what is not here: no specificity score, no counts. The claim rests on reading twenty descriptions, which fits the paper's [[dictionary-resolution]] picture of dictionaries as zoom levels on a fixed set of [[true-features]], but is presented as an example, not a measurement.

terms.definition: The coarsest dictionary learning run shown, with 512 learned features. The 'A' names the transformer, the '0' the run; all three runs here use the same L1 coefficient and differ only in dictionary size.
The middle run, with 4,096 learned features. This is the run the paper focuses on most elsewhere.
The finest run shown, with 16,384 learned features. Not the largest the paper trained, just the largest in this comparison.
The coarse feature at top left: mathematical terminology and notation related to abstract algebra, especially homomorphisms, isomorphisms and topological spaces. Its descendants are drawn in pink.
The coarse feature at bottom left: 'the' in mathematical prose. A token-in-context feature — one specific token, but only in one kind of surrounding text. Its descendants are drawn in purple.
A middle-run feature: mathematical quantifiers in a LaTeX context. A refinement of A/0/281 that keys on quantifier words rather than algebraic terminology generally.
A middle-run feature: mathematical prose, especially in topology and abstract algebra (the figure prints 'toplogy'). It keeps most of A/0/281's subject matter but drops the notation emphasis.
A middle-run feature: 'the' in physics, especially field theory. Descends from A/0/281 despite that parent being described in mathematical rather than physics terms.
A middle-run feature: 'the' when preceding a term in physics, especially condensed matter physics. Sits alongside A/1/3362 as a second, differently-flavoured physics 'the'.
A middle-run feature: 'a' in the context of math. It is the one box in the figure with two parents, receiving both a pink line from A/0/281 and a purple line from A/0/341.
A middle-run feature: 'the' and occasionally words after 'the' in machine learning. A domain-specific slice of the generic mathematical 'the'.
A middle-run feature: 'the' in mathematics, especially topology and complex analysis. In A/2 this splits into separate topology and complex-analysis features.
A fine-run feature: 'every' and 'each' in mathematical prose. One of two children of the LaTeX-quantifier feature A/1/437, keyed to specific quantifier words.
A fine-run feature: quantity-related words in mathematical prose. The other child of A/1/437.
A fine-run feature: mathematical prose, especially in category theory. The sole drawn child of A/1/491, narrowing topology-and-algebra to one subfield.
A fine-run feature: 'the' in math and technical writing. A child of the field-theory feature A/1/3362.

A fine-run feature: prepositions in physics and technical writing. The paper cites it as a gravitation-and-field-theory feature whose top logit predictions include 'the gauge', 'the Lagrangian' and 'the spacetime'.
A fine-run feature: 'the' and occasionally words after 'the' in mathematical prose. The sole drawn child of the condensed-matter feature A/1/1652.
A fine-run feature: 'a' in mathematical equations as a variable, with some firing as a preposition in the bottom activations. A child of A/1/512 that distinguishes 'a'-as-symbol from 'a'-as-article.
A fine-run feature: 'a' in mathematical prose, often following equations. The other child of A/1/512, covering the article rather than the variable.

A fine-run feature: 'the' and occasionally words after 'the' in machine learning. The paper names it as the finely split machine-learning version of A/0/341, with top logit predictions like 'the dataset' and 'the classifier'.
A fine-run feature: 'the' in mathematics, especially complex analysis. One of two children of A/1/1638.
A fine-run feature: 'the' in mathematics, especially topology and abstract algebra. The paper reports its top logit predictions include 'the quotient' and 'the subgroup'.
The edges tracing descendants of A/0/281 through A/1 and into A/2. Colour marks which coarse feature a branch comes from and carries no other meaning.
The edges tracing descendants of A/0/341. Where a pink and a purple line reach the same box, that feature descends from both coarse features.

The measure that decides whether two features across runs get a line. Cosine similarity between their activation vectors, computed twice — once over only the tokens where the first fires, once over only the tokens where the second fires — keeping the larger value.
The phenomenon the figure illustrates: as the dictionary grows, a feature is replaced by a family of narrower features covering roughly the same territory.
Features firing on fewer than roughly one token in a million, almost none of them interpretable. The paper excludes them before building this graph.

numbers.meaning: The number of learned features in A/0, the leftmost column. It equals the transformer's MLP width, so this dictionary is not overcomplete — one learned feature per neuron, an expansion factor of 1x.
The number of learned features in A/1, the middle column. Eight times the MLP width.

The number of learned features in A/2, the rightmost column. Thirty-two times the MLP width. The three sizes are powers of two chosen as a sweep with the L1 coefficient held fixed, so column-to-column differences come from dictionary size alone.

The masked cosine similarity threshold above which a line is drawn between two features. The paper says plainly it was chosen for display — low enough to show some of the richness of splitting, high enough to keep the graph visualisable. Nothing about the value is derived.

The number of boxes drawn in the A/0, A/1 and A/2 columns. These are the features linked above threshold, not counts of all math-related features in each run; the surrounding text says the coarsest run has three features for technical settings, while the figure as printed traces two.

The feature indices inside each run. They are arbitrary identifiers assigned by the autoencoder's hidden-unit ordering, so index size carries no meaning — A/1/512 sharing a number with A/0's dictionary size is a coincidence.

The parallel count the paper gives for base64 features across the same three runs, quoted in the section this figure sits in. It is the same sweep read on a different feature family, and is why the paper treats splitting as general rather than particular to mathematics.
The widest autoencoder in the paper's full sweep, given for context. This figure stops at 16,384, so it shows part of the range rather than its end.
